messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Entrapment: Having no options, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Nguyen was 80 years old when he first came for help, a widowed South Eastern Asian man who had built a second career as a data scientist after a long life marked by migration, work, and loss. He spoke in a measured way, but with a strain beneath the surface that became more visible as he described the years since he had served as a relief worker in a war zone. During that assignment, he had gone into damaged neighborhoods to help distribute supplies and record needs, moving through streets where ordinary choices had been stripped away by fighting. He remembered one particular day when he and several others were trapped in a building for hours, unable to leave because the roads were unsafe and the options kept narrowing as the shelling came closer. He described the sickening sense of having no way out, of being forced to wait while other people made violent decisions around him. In the same period, he had seen people behave in ways he experienced as deeply wrong, turning on one another, taking what was meant for families, and abandoning the vulnerable. That moral violation stayed with him as sharply as the fear of the guns. Even now, the details of that time return with unusual force. When Minh remembers the frightening event, he does not feel as though it belongs to the past; he said it is like the scene is happening right now, and that the memory plays in his mind like a film that starts again without warning. He can be sitting quietly and then suddenly feel pulled back into the room where he had been trapped, with the same immediate sense of danger and pressure.

After he returned to the United States, he tried to settle into ordinary routines, but certain moments repeatedly brought the war zone back into the present. He noticed that waking up from a nightmare was especially unsettling, because for a few seconds after opening his eyes he could not tell whether he was in his own apartment or back in that building with no exit. He would wake tense, disoriented, and already bracing for something terrible. He also found himself recoiling from news reports about events similar to what had happened to him. If a television in a café or waiting room showed images of conflict, displacement, or civilian suffering, he would leave or turn away, saying he did not need to “go back there” through the screen. Over time, he became known among friends and colleagues as someone who prepared obsessively for any conversation. Before meetings at work, before speaking to a neighbor, even before answering a phone call, he rehearsed what he would say. Minh explained that he wanted to avoid saying the wrong thing or sounding confused, because he was frightened that his reactions since the war meant he was going crazy. He watched himself closely for signs that he might lose control, and that fear extended to anger as well. He worried that if something pushed him too far, he would not be able to control his rage and might do something terrible.

Minh’s daily life had become organized around scanning for danger. As a data scientist, he still worked with numbers and screens, but even at his desk he would constantly check the environment around him, noting exits, hallways, who was standing too close, and whether anything seemed off. In restaurants, on the bus, and in the lobby of his building, his attention kept moving outward, searching for threat even when he knew, intellectually, that he was in a safe place. He described feeling constantly tense and ready to react, as if his body refused to stand down. This state left him irritable, and he acknowledged that he had snapped at people more easily in recent years. Small frustrations could set him on edge, and he sometimes heard himself speaking in a harder tone than he intended. That made him withdraw further. Since his wife’s death, the apartment had grown quieter, and he had fewer chances to be distracted from his own vigilance. He continued to function, but in a narrower and more effortful way, with more energy spent on holding himself together and on avoiding reminders of the war.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was the growing exhaustion of living this way and the worry that the intensity of his reactions was no longer something he could simply endure in silence. He was troubled by the way he woke from nightmares already shaken, by how quickly his mind replayed the past as though it were unfolding again, and by the sense that the world had become permanently dangerous. More than anything, he wanted to know whether he was truly losing his mind or whether there was a way to feel safe enough to stop scanning every room and rehearsing every sentence.
